ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 8 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 80000.

Now the 8 in the hundreds place. That seat is worth 100, so 8 times 100 is 800.

We need to write 1945 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 1000, 900, 40 and 5.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.
1000 is simply M.
Now the 900. How do the Romans write 900?

ask.ifNot: C in front of M takes 100 away from 1000, which leaves 900. C after M would add 100 on instead.

beats.say: 900 is 100 less than 1000, so the smaller letter goes in front: C M.
40 is 10 less than 50, so the smaller letter goes in front: X L. 5 is simply V.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: M, C M, X L, V.
Careful with the tens as well. X before L is 40. Turn them round to L X and you have made 60.

We need to write 1946 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.

Here is a number with two stars in it. Both stars hide the same digit, and we want the difference between their place values.

board.text: 6★74★3: difference of the two ★ place values

beats.say: First find the seats. From the right: 3 is in the ones, a star is in the tens, 4 is in the hundreds and 7 is in the thousands. Where is the other star?

ask.ifNot: Count on from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, and then ten-thousands. That is where the second star sits.

The plan: find the two seats, test with a 1 to see the pattern, then look for the choice that fits.
Here is 7,02,459. We swap the 5 and the 0, and then find the difference between the new number and the old one.

ask.ifNot: Compare the ten-thousands digits. The new number has 5 there and the old one has 0, so the new number is bigger.

But the tens seat went from 5 down to 0, so the number lost 50. That is the part people forget!
So the difference is 50000 minus 50, which is 49950.
Check by subtracting the whole numbers. 7,52,409 minus 7,02,459 is 49950 as well.
So when two digits swap, just look at the seats that changed: what was gained, and what was lost.
There are two jobs here. First find the greatest of these 5 numbers. Then find the place value of the 6 in it.

46749 or 47659: which one is greater?

Two years, written in Roman numerals. To find how long the company ran, we turn both into our numbers, subtract, and turn the answer back.

board.text: Began MCDXLIX, closed MDCLXV. How long?

beats.say: The closing year starts M, then D C. D is 500 and C is 100. What is D C worth?

ask.ifNot: Here the bigger letter D comes first, so we add: 500 and 100 make 600. Only C D, the other way round, is 400.

So the closing year is 1000, 600, 60 and 5. That makes 1665.

Back to Roman. 216 is 200, 10 and 6. That is C C, then X, then V I.
So the plan: read each numeral in parts, do the sum in our own numbers, then write the answer in Roman letters.

board.text: Greatest 3-digit even − smallest 3-digit odd, in Roman

ask.ifNot: Step down just one from 999. 998 ends in 8, so it is even, and it still has 3 digits.

ask.ifNot: 0 is the smallest digit, but a number cannot start with 0. So the first seat takes the next smallest digit, which is 2.

board.text: 20479: the 9 is in the ones place

board.text: Greatest − smallest 4-digit number, all digits different

beats.say: For the greatest, start with the biggest digit, 9, and step down: 9, 8, 7, 6. That makes 9876.

In 7,26,935, one digit has a place value that is exactly 10,000 times its face value. Let us find that digit.

board.text: 7,26,935: place value = 10,000 × face value. Which digit?

board.text: place value = face value × worth of the seat

beats.say: So we want the seat that is worth 10,000. Which place is that?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. The fifth seat is worth 10,000.

beats.say: Now count the seats of 7,26,935 from the right: 5 ones, 3 tens, 9 hundreds, 6 thousands, 2 ten-thousands.
So the digit is 2. Its place value is 20,000, which is 2 times 10,000.

The international system groups the digits from the right. How many digits go in each group?

ask.ifNot: The Indian system goes 3, then 2, then 2. The international system keeps it simple: 3 digits in every group.

beats.say: So group in threes from the right. We get 30, then 540, then 3 zeros.

target.text: Thirty million five hundred forty thousand

Rahim gets 3,00,000 rupees, all in 100 rupee notes. We want to know how many notes that is.
Each note is worth 100. Which sum tells us the number of notes?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many hundreds fit into 3,00,000. Finding how many fit is a division.

beats.say: So we divide 3,00,000 by 100.
First count the zeros in 3,00,000. There are 5 of them.
Dividing by 100 takes away 2 zeros, one for each zero in 100. So 5 zeros become 3 zeros.
A 3 with 3 zeros is 3,000. So Rahim gets 3,000 notes.
Check: 3,000 notes of 100 rupees make 3,00,000 rupees. It works.
Careful when you count the zeros in a lakh. 1 lakh has 5 zeros, not 4. Miss one, and the answer comes out ten times too small.
India became independent in the year M C M X L V I I. We want the year 75 years later, in Roman numerals.
Roman numerals are hard to add. So first, we change the year into our own numbers, part by part.
C M has a smaller letter in front of a bigger one. C is 100 and M is 1000. So what is C M?

ask.ifNot: A smaller letter in front is taken away. 1000 minus 100 is 900.

beats.say: So M is 1000, C M is 900, X L is 40 and V I I is 7. The year is 1947.
Now add 75 years. 1947 plus 75 is 2022.
Back to Roman letters. 2022 is 2000, 20 and 2.
2000 is M M. 20 is X X. And 2 is I I.
Careful: we crossed the year 2000, so the answer has to start with M M. A numeral starting M C M is still before 2000.
So: Roman to our numbers, do the sum, then back to Roman.
4 Roman numerals to put in order, smallest first. They look alike, so let us find the value of each one.

board.text: XL, LX, XIV, XLIV: smallest first

beats.say: X L has the smaller letter first, so we take away. 50 minus 10 is 40.
Now L X. The bigger letter is first this time. What is L X worth?

ask.ifNot: When the bigger letter comes first, we add. 50 and 10 make 60.

beats.say: L X is 50 plus 10, which is 60. The same letters as X L, but a different number!
X I V is 10, and then I V, which is 4. That makes 14.
X L I V is X L, which is 40, and then I V, which is 4. That makes 44.
Now put the numbers in order: 14, 40, 44, 60.
So in Roman numerals, smallest first: X I V, then X L, then X L I V, then L X.
The trap is X L I V. It begins like X L, so it is 44, and it comes before L X, not after it.
Some number was rounded to the nearest hundred, and the result was 4,700. We want the greatest whole number it could have been.
Numbers above 4,700 can round down to it, as long as they are closer to 4,700 than to 4,800.
Halfway between them is 4,750. Which way does the halfway number round?

ask.ifNot: The rule is: 5 or more in the tens place rounds up. 4,750 has a 5 in the tens place, so it rounds up to 4,800.

beats.say: So 4,750 is already too big, because it rounds up to 4,800. That is the trap in this question.
Step back just one. 4,749 has a 4 in the tens place, and 4 is less than 5, so it rounds down to 4,700.
So the greatest whole number is 4,749.
And what about 4,799? It is far too close to 4,800. Only the tens digit matters: 4 or less rounds down, 5 or more rounds up.
So for the greatest number that rounds down: go to the halfway point, then step back one.
38,462 people watched the match. Anil rounds to the nearest thousand and Bina rounds to the nearest ten. How far apart are their answers?

board.text: 38,462: nearest thousand, and nearest ten. Difference?

beats.say: Anil rounds to the nearest thousand. Which digit must he look at to decide?

ask.ifNot: To round to a place, look at the digit just to its right. For thousands, that is the hundreds digit, which is 4.

beats.say: The hundreds digit is 4. That is less than 5, so Anil rounds down to 38,000.
Bina rounds to the nearest ten, so she looks at the ones digit. It is 2, less than 5, so she rounds down to 38,460.
Now the difference: 38,460 minus 38,000 is 460.
Careful: use Bina's rounded number, 38,460, not the number we started with. Otherwise you get 462.
So for each rounding, look one digit to the right. Less than 5, go down. 5 or more, go up.
Two words to know here. The successor of a number is the one just after it. The predecessor is the one just before it.

board.text: Successor of greatest 4-digit + predecessor of smallest

beats.say: The greatest 4-digit number is 9,999. Its successor is 1 more. What is 9,999 plus 1?

ask.ifNot: Adding 1 turns every 9 into a 0 and puts a new 1 in front. So we get 10,000, which has 5 digits.

beats.say: 9,999 plus 1 is 10,000. Every 9 rolls over to 0.
The smallest 4-digit number is 1,000. Its predecessor is 1 less, which is 999.
Now add the two: 10,000 plus 999 is 10,999.
Careful with the two words. Successor goes up one, predecessor goes down one. Mix them up and you add a different pair of numbers.
So: find each special number, take one step the right way, then add.
We are told the successor of a secret number is 20,000. We want the predecessor of that same secret number.
The successor is one more than the number. So where is the secret number?

ask.ifNot: 20,000 comes just after the secret number. So the secret number is one step back from 20,000.

beats.say: One step back from 20,000 is 19,999. That is our secret number.
Careful: we are not done! 19,999 is the number itself. The question asks for its predecessor, one more step back.
So from a successor back to the predecessor is always 2 steps. 20,000 minus 2 is 19,998.
Predecessor, number, successor: three neighbours in a row.
We want the greatest 4-digit number whose digits are all different and add up to 10.

board.text: 4 different digits that add up to 10. Greatest number?

beats.say: For a big number, the first digit should be as big as possible. So try 9 first. The other 3 digits must then add up to 1.
Three different digits that add up to 1. Can it be done?

ask.ifNot: 1, 0 and 0 does add up to 1, but the 0 is used twice. The digits must all be different, so 9 cannot go first.

beats.say: So 9 is out. Try 8: the rest must add up to 2. That needs 2, 0, 0 or 1, 1, 0. A digit repeats each time, so 8 is out too.
Now try 7. The rest must add up to 3, and 2, 1 and 0 do it. All different!
Put those digits after the 7, from greatest to smallest. That makes 7210.
Check: 7 plus 2 plus 1 plus 0 is 10, and no digit repeats.
The trap is 9100. Its digits add up to 10, but the 0 is used twice. Read every rule in the question.
In 46,285 the digit 6 is swapped for a 9. By how much does the number grow?
Count from the right: 5 ones, 8 tens, 2 hundreds. Where is the 6?

ask.ifNot: 5 is in the ones, 8 is in the tens, 2 is in the hundreds, and next comes the 6, in the thousands place.

beats.say: The 6 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 6,000.
A 9 in the same seat is worth 9,000.
Nothing else changed. So the number grows by 9,000 minus 6,000, which is 3,000.
Careful: 9 minus 6 is only 3. But these are 3 thousands, because of the seat the digit sits in.
Check with the whole numbers: 49,285 minus 46,285 is 3,000.
Riya writes every number from 1 to 100. We count how many times her pencil writes the digit 7.

board.text: Numbers 1 to 100: how many times is the digit 7 written?

beats.say: A 7 can be in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place on its own. First the ones: 7, 17, 27, and so on, up to 97.
That is 10 numbers, so the 7 is written 10 times in the ones place.
Now the tens place. Which numbers have a 7 in the tens place?

ask.ifNot: A 7 in the tens place means the number is in the seventies. That is every number from 70 to 79.

beats.say: From 70 to 79 there are 10 numbers, so that is 10 more sevens.
Here is the trap: 77. It is in both lists! But that is right, because 77 really has two 7s, and both are written.
So the total is 10 plus 10, which is 20.
So when you count a digit, count one place at a time. A number like 77 is counted once in each place.
A number puzzle with 5 seats. Two clues are easy: 3 goes in the ten-thousands place and 0 goes in the hundreds place.
The ones digit is the greatest odd digit. The odd digits are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, so the ones digit is 9.
Now the tricky clue: the thousands digit is twice the tens digit. The pairs could be 2 and 1, 4 and 2, 6 and 3, or 8 and 4.
One of those pairs breaks the rule that all 5 digits are different. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Look at what is already in the number: 3, 0 and 9. The pair 6 and 3 would use the 3 a second time.

beats.say: So 6 and 3 is out, because 3 is already in the first seat.
We want the greatest number, so choose the biggest thousands digit that is left. That is 8, with 4 in the tens.
The number is 38049.
Check every clue: 8 is twice 4, the ones digit is 9, 0 is in the hundreds, and 3, 8, 0, 4, 9 are all different.
Careful with 38409. It uses the same digits, but the 0 has slipped out of the hundreds place.

board.text: 38409: 0 is not in the hundreds place

beats.say: We want the smallest 5-digit number that is odd and has no digit repeated. Build it one seat at a time, from the left.

board.text: Smallest 5-digit odd number, all digits different = ?

beats.say: The first seat cannot be 0, so it takes 1. The second seat can take 0, the smallest digit of all.
Next come the smallest digits not used yet: 2, and then 3.
Now the last seat. The number must be odd, and no digit may repeat. Which digit goes there?

ask.ifNot: 4 would make the number even. 1 and 3 are odd, but they are already used. So the smallest odd digit left is 5.

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. But 1 and 3 are taken, so we use 5.
The number is 10235.
Careful: 10234 is the smallest with different digits, but it is even. And 12345 forgets that 0 can sit in the second seat.
Which of these 4 numbers needs the most letters when it is written in Roman numerals? Let us write each one and count.

board.text: 99, 98, 88, 78: which needs the most Roman symbols?

beats.say: First, a question. Is the biggest number always the longest in Roman numerals?

choices: No, some big numbers are short
ask.ifNot: Think of 10. It is just X. But 8 is V I I I, which is much longer. Bigger does not mean longer.

beats.say: 99 is 90 and 9. That is X C and I X. Only 4 letters, thanks to the take away trick.
98 is 90 and 8. That is X C and V I I I, which makes 6 letters.
78 is 70 and 8. That is L X X and V I I I, which makes 7 letters.
88 is 80 and 8. That is L X X X and V I I I, which makes 8 letters. The longest of all!
So the answer is 88.
The lesson: 8s make a numeral long, because an 8 needs 4 letters. 9s and 4s keep it short.
Meena does not know the take away rule. She just adds up all four letters of X L I V. How much bigger is her total than the true value?

board.text: XLIV: Meena adds X, L, I and V. How much too big?

beats.say: First, Meena's way. X is 10, L is 50, I is 1 and V is 5. She adds them all and gets 66.
Now the true value. In X L, the smaller letter X is in front of L. What does that mean?

ask.ifNot: A smaller letter in front of a bigger one is taken away. So X L is 50 minus 10.

beats.say: X L is 50 minus 10, which is 40. And I V is 5 minus 1, which is 4.
So the true value is 40 plus 4, which is 44.
Now compare. Meena's 66 minus the true 44 is 22.
Careful: 66 and 44 are both among the choices, but neither is what the question asks. It asks how much greater.
A neat check: each letter in front was added when it should be taken away, so it counts double. Twice 10 plus twice 1 is 22.
Lots of numbers round to 600 when we round to the nearest hundred. We want to count all of them.

board.text: How many whole numbers round to 600 (nearest hundred)?

beats.say: Numbers below 600 can round up to it. What is the smallest number that rounds up to 600?

ask.ifNot: A 5 in the tens place is enough to round up, and 550 has a 5 there. Anything smaller rounds down to 500 instead.

beats.say: The smallest is 550, because a 5 in the tens place rounds up.
Numbers above 600 round down while the tens digit is 4 or less. So the greatest is 649. The next one, 650, rounds up to 700.
Now count from 550 to 649. Subtract first: 649 minus 550 is 99.
Careful, this is the trap! Subtracting counts the steps, not the numbers. We add 1 so that both ends are counted.
So 100 whole numbers round to 600.
That makes sense: 50 numbers from 550 to 599, and 50 more from 600 to 649.
A number rounds to 350 to the nearest ten, and to 300 to the nearest hundred. We want the greatest number that does both.
Take the first clue. The numbers that round to 350, to the nearest ten, run from 345 up to 354.
Now the second clue. To the nearest hundred, where does 350 itself go?

ask.ifNot: 350 has a 5 in the tens place, and 5 or more rounds up. So 350 goes up to 400.

beats.say: So 350, and anything above it, rounds to 400 and not 300. Only the numbers below 350 are left.
The numbers that fit both clues are 345, 346, 347, 348 and 349.
The greatest of these is 349.
Check: 349 to the nearest ten is 350. And 349 to the nearest hundred is 300. Both clues fit.
The trap is 354. It is the greatest number that rounds to 350, but it does not fit the second clue.
Sana and Ravi both start with 4,446. Sana rounds 3 times, one step at a time. Ravi rounds just once. Will they end at the same number?

board.text: 4,446: Sana rounds in 3 steps, Ravi rounds once

beats.say: Sana first rounds to the nearest ten. The ones digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so she goes up to 4,450.
Next she rounds 4,450 to the nearest hundred. The tens digit is 5. Which way does she go?

ask.ifNot: 5 or more rounds up. The tens digit is exactly 5, so 4,450 goes up to 4,500.

beats.say: Up to 4,500. Then she rounds that to the nearest thousand. The hundreds digit is now 5, so up again, to 5,000.
Now Ravi. He rounds 4,446 straight to the nearest thousand. The hundreds digit is 4, less than 5, so he goes down to 4,000.
The difference is 5,000 minus 4,000, which is 1,000.
Here is the surprise. Each little rounding pushed Sana's number up a bit, until it tipped over. Rounding in steps can change the answer.
So always round straight from the number you started with. Ravi's way is the proper one.
A printer numbers the pages from 1 to 120. Some page numbers have 1 digit, some have 2 and some have 3. So we count in three groups.

board.text: Pages 1 to 120: how many digits are printed?

beats.say: Pages 1 to 9 have 1 digit each. That is 9 pages, so 9 digits.
Pages 10 to 99 have 2 digits each. How many pages is that?

ask.ifNot: There are 99 pages up to page 99. Take away the first 9 pages, and 90 pages are left.

beats.say: 90 pages with 2 digits each is 180 digits.
Now pages 100 to 120. Careful, this is the trap. 120 minus 100 is 20, but there are 21 pages, because page 100 counts too.
21 pages with 3 digits each is 63 digits.
Add the three groups: 9 plus 180 plus 63 is 252.
So: split the pages into groups by how many digits they have, and count both ends of every group.
Take a 2-digit number, swap its digits, and add the two. The total must be 121. How many numbers can do that?

board.text: Number + its reverse = 121. How many 2-digit numbers?

beats.say: Try one to see what happens. 29 plus 92 is 121. It works! And look at its digits: 2 plus 9 is 11.
Here is why. In the ones column we add the two digits. In the tens column we add the same two digits again. So the total is 11 times the digit sum.
So what must the two digits add up to, for a total of 121?

ask.ifNot: The total is 11 times the digit sum. 11 times 11 is 121, so the digits must add up to 11.

beats.say: The digits must add up to 11. List the pairs: 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6.
Careful, this is the trap. Each pair makes two numbers, like 29 and 92. So 4 pairs give 8 numbers.
So 8 different numbers work.
And why not start with 1? Its partner would have to be 10, and 10 is not a digit.
A number like 2552 reads the same forwards and backwards. We want the greatest 4-digit one whose digits add up to 14.

board.text: Reads the same both ways, digits add up to 14. Greatest?

beats.say: Such a number has a matching outer pair and a matching inner pair.
The 4 digits add up to 14. Each digit is there twice, so one outer digit and one inner digit add up to half of 14, which is 7.
For the greatest number, which digit should be as big as possible?

ask.ifNot: The outer digit sits in the thousands place, the most powerful seat. So make the outer digit as big as you can.

beats.say: The outer digit can be as big as 7. That leaves 0 for the inner digit, and 0 is allowed in the middle.
So the number is 7007.
Check: 7 plus 0 plus 0 plus 7 is 14, and 7007 reads the same both ways.
Two traps here. 6116 fits the clues, but it is smaller. And 7700 adds up to 14, but backwards it is not the same.
In 8,35,264 we count the digits whose place value is more than 100 times their face value.

board.text: 8,35,264: digits with place value > 100 × face value?

beats.say: Place value is face value times the worth of the seat. So this is really about seats: which seats are worth more than 100?
The 2 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 200. That is exactly 100 times 2. Does it count?

choices: No, exactly 100 is not more than 100
ask.ifNot: The question says more than 100 times. The 2 is worth exactly 100 times its face value, and exactly is not more.

beats.say: This is the trap. Exactly 100 times is not more than 100 times. So the 2 is out, and so are the 6 in the tens and the 4 in the ones.
The seats worth more than 100 are the thousands, ten-thousands and lakhs. The digits sitting there are 5, 3 and 8.
That is 3 digits.
Check one of them: the 5 is worth 5,000, which is 1,000 times 5. Yes, that is more than 100 times.
So: turn the clue into seats, and read little words like more than very carefully.
Among the Roman numerals from 1 to 39, some are written with exactly 2 letters. We count them in an orderly way.

board.text: Roman numerals 1 to 39: how many use exactly 2 letters?

beats.say: Only 3 letters are used up to 39: I, V and X. Let us sort the 2-letter numerals by their first letter.
Starting with I: I I is 2, I V is 4 and I X is 9. That is 3 numerals.
Starting with V, there is V I, which is 6. Is V V a proper numeral as well?

ask.ifNot: Two fives make 10, and 10 already has its own letter, X. So V is never written twice.

beats.say: So V gives just one numeral, V I. And V X is not allowed either, because V is never used to take away.
Starting with X: X I is 11, X V is 15 and X X is 20. That is 3 more.
Careful: X L has 2 letters too. But X L is 40, and that is outside 1 to 39.
Add them up: 3 plus 1 plus 3 is 7.
So when you count, sort into groups, and check the edges of the range.
We add something to 49,950, and we want its ten-thousands digit to change. What is the smallest number that does it?
The ten-thousands digit is 4 now. Counting up, which is the first number with a different ten-thousands digit?

ask.ifNot: As we count up from 49,950, the 4 in front stays until all the other seats are full. It first changes at 50,000.

beats.say: The 4 changes to a 5 the moment we reach 50,000.
So how far is 49,950 from 50,000? Subtract.
Just 50! The number was already very close.
Check: 49,950 plus 50 is 50,000. And adding anything less, like 49, stays below 50,000.
The trap is to think a big seat needs a big number, like 10,000. But the question asks for the smallest.

board.text: 10,000 works, but it is not the smallest

beats.say: Rahul writes a 6-digit number using only the digits 3, 0 and 8. Each must appear at least once. We want the greatest number.

board.text: 6 digits, only 3, 0 and 8, each used at least once

beats.say: At least once. Does that mean a digit can be used more than once?

choices: Yes, as many times as we like
ask.ifNot: At least once means once or more. And we need 6 digits from only 3 kinds, so some digit has to repeat.

beats.say: So digits may repeat. For the greatest number, we want the biggest digit, 8, in as many seats on the left as possible.
But 3 and 0 must each appear once. So they take 2 seats, and 8 fills the other 4.
Now the last two seats. The tens seat is worth more than the ones seat, so the bigger digit, 3, goes in the tens.
The greatest number is 888830.
Careful with 888803. It is very close, but the 3 and the 0 are the other way round, and that makes it smaller.
So: fill the big seats with the big digit, and give the small digits the smallest seats.
We want to count the odd numbers from 20 to 50. Counting them one by one would take a while, so let us be clever.

board.text: Odd numbers from 20 to 50: how many?

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. 20 and 50 are both even, so the first odd number is 21 and the last is 49.
Odd and even numbers take turns. So in any 10 numbers in a row, how many are odd?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even take turns, so exactly half of them are odd. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Look at the 10 numbers from 21 to 30. The odd ones are 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29. That is 5 of them.
From 21 to 50 there are 3 lots of ten like that. So we need 3 lots of 5.
3 times 5 is 15. So there are 15 odd numbers.
Let us check another way. From 21 to 49 we jump in twos. 49 minus 21 is 28, and half of 28 is 14 jumps.
Careful here: 14 jumps touch 15 numbers, because the starting number counts too. So it is 15 again.
So the plan: find the first and last odd number, then count in tens, 5 odd numbers for every ten.
We want to count the odd numbers from 50 to 90. Counting them one by one would take a while, so let us be clever.

board.text: Odd numbers from 50 to 90: how many?

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. 50 and 90 are both even, so the first odd number is 51 and the last is 89.
Odd and even numbers take turns. So in any 10 numbers in a row, how many are odd?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even take turns, so exactly half of them are odd. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Look at the 10 numbers from 51 to 60. The odd ones are 51, 53, 55, 57 and 59. That is 5 of them.
From 51 to 90 there are 4 lots of ten like that. So we need 4 lots of 5.
4 times 5 is 20. So there are 20 odd numbers.
Let us check another way. From 51 to 89 we jump in twos. 89 minus 51 is 38, and half of 38 is 19 jumps.
Careful here: 19 jumps touch 20 numbers, because the starting number counts too. So it is 20 again.
So the plan: find the first and last odd number, then count in tens, 5 odd numbers for every ten.
Each of these numbers has two 6s. We want the number where one 6 is worth 1000 times the other 6.

board.text: One 6 worth 1000 times the other 6: in which number?

beats.say: Each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right. So how many seats apart must the two 6s be?

ask.ifNot: One seat apart is 10 times. Two seats is 100 times. Three seats is 1000 times. So the 6s must be 3 seats apart.

board.text: 1 seat left: 10 times      2 seats left: 100 times

beats.say: 10 times 10 times 10 is 1000. So we look for two 6s that are 3 seats apart.
Take 576006. One 6 is in the thousands, worth 6000. The other is in the ones, worth 6. Yes, 3 seats apart!
Now the trap. Do not stop at the first one that fits! One of the choices is All of them, so we must test the others too.
In 567060 the 6s are worth 60000 and 60. That fits as well.
In 657600 the 6s are worth 600000 and 600. That fits too.
All three numbers work. So the answer is: All of them.
Remember: when All of them is a choice, test every number before you decide.
We write the Roman numerals from 1 to 20, and count every V we write.

board.text: Roman numerals I to XX: how many times is V written?

beats.say: First, 1 to 10. The numerals with a V are I V, V, V I, V I I and V I I I. Those are 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8.
What about 9? Is there a V in the numeral for 9?

choices: Yes, 9 is V I I I I
ask.ifNot: A letter is never written 4 times in a row. 9 is 1 less than 10, so it is I X, with no V at all.

beats.say: 9 is I X, so there is no V there. That gives 5 Vs from 1 to 10.
From 11 to 20 the same pattern repeats with an X in front: X I V, X V, X V I, X V I I and X V I I I.
Careful: the sneaky ones are I V and X I V, where the V hides behind an I. And X I X and X X have no V at all.
So 5 plus 5 makes 10.
So: write out the pattern for 1 to 10, then see how it repeats for the next ten.
We need to write 1946 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 1000, 900, 40 and 6.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.
1000 is simply M.
Now the 900. How do the Romans write 900?

ask.ifNot: C in front of M takes 100 away from 1000, which leaves 900. C after M would add 100 on instead.

beats.say: 900 is 100 less than 1000, so the smaller letter goes in front: C M.
40 is 10 less than 50, so the smaller letter goes in front: X L. 6 is 5 and 1 more, so we write V I.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: M, C M, X L, V I.
Check the tens carefully. X X X is only 30. For 40 we need X L.
So the plan for any number: split it by place, write each part in Roman letters, then join them from left to right.
We need to write this number name in figures. Let us take it one piece at a time.

board.text: One lakh one thousand one hundred ten = ?

beats.say: One lakh is a 1 followed by 5 zeros.
One thousand is 1,000. And one hundred ten is 110.
Now add the three pieces together.
Look at the thousands. They have 2 seats, but there is only one thousand. What goes in those 2 seats?

ask.ifNot: One thousand needs a 1 in the thousands seat. The ten-thousands seat is empty, so it gets a 0 to hold the place.

beats.say: That 0 is a place holder. Leave it out, or put a 1 there, and the number changes.
So the number is 1,01,110. Without the commas, that is 101110.
Check: it has 6 digits, just as a lakh number should.
M N is a 2-digit number with tens digit M and units digit N. N M is the same two digits swapped. We want the biggest possible difference.

board.text: M and N: different digits, not zero

beats.say: To make a difference big, the first number should be as big as we can make it, and the second as small as we can.
For a big M N, the tens digit M should be the biggest digit there is, 9.
Now N should be as small as the rules allow. What is the smallest N we may use?

ask.ifNot: 0 is the smallest digit, but the question says the digits are not zero. So the smallest N allowed is 1.

beats.say: This is the trap. The digits are non zero, so N cannot be 0. The smallest it can be is 1.
So M N is 91 and N M is 19.
91 minus 19 is 72.
A pattern to notice: the difference is always 9 times the gap between the digits. The gap here is 8, and 9 times 8 is 72.
In 978652 we want the place value of the 7, the place value of the 5, and then the difference between them.

board.text: 978652: place value of 7 − place value of 5 = ?

beats.say: Count from the right: 2 ones, 5 tens, 6 hundreds, 8 thousands, and then the 7. Which place is the 7 in?

ask.ifNot: After the thousands comes the ten-thousands place. The 7 is the fifth digit from the right, so it sits there.

beats.say: So the 7 is worth 70000.
The 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 50.
Difference means subtract. So we need 70000 minus 50.
Borrowing across all those zeros is fiddly. Try this instead: 70000 minus 100 is 69900. Then give back 50.
So the difference is 69950.
Careful: 70050 is what you get by adding. The word difference always means take away.
Three Roman numerals. Only a numeral that follows every rule is correctly written. So let us check each one against the rules.

board.text: Which Roman numeral is correctly written?

beats.say: Rule one: a letter may be repeated at most 3 times in a row.

board.text: Rule 1: a letter repeats at most 3 times

beats.say: Look at M C C C C I V. Does it follow rule one?

ask.ifNot: Count the Cs. There are 4 in a row, and that breaks the rule.

beats.say: 4 Cs in a row, so that one is out. 400 should be written C D.
Rule two: V, L and D are never put in front of a bigger letter to take away.

board.text: Rule 2: V, L, D never go in front to take away

beats.say: In C D V L I I, the V stands in front of L. That breaks rule two, so it is out as well.
Now C D L X V I. C D is 400, then L is 50, X is 10, V is 5 and I is 1. Every part follows the rules. It is 466.
So do not rush to None of these. Test each numeral against the rules, one at a time.
m stands for some even number and n stands for some odd number. We must find which of the 4 expressions is always odd.

board.text: m is even, n is odd. Which is always odd?

beats.say: We do not know m and n, so let us test with easy numbers. Take m as 2 and n as 1.
First, 3 m plus 4 n. 3 times 2 is 6, 4 times 1 is 4, and 6 plus 4 is 10. That is even.
Now m plus 3 n. With m as 2 and n as 1, what do we get?

ask.ifNot: 3 n is 3 times 1, which is 3. Then 2 plus 3 is 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5, and 5 is odd. That looks like our answer.
Check the other two. 5 m plus 6 n is 10 plus 6, which is 16. And 5 m n is 5 times 2 times 1, which is 10. Both are even.
Why does it always work? m is even. 3 n is odd times odd, which is odd. And even plus odd is always odd.
So the answer is m plus 3 n.
The key idea: anything times an even number is even. So look for the expression with exactly one odd part.
Four Roman numerals, and we want the largest. But be careful: not all of them are proper numerals.

board.text: Which Roman numeral has the largest value?

beats.say: Look at X X X X I X. It has X four times in a row. Is that allowed?

choices: No, at most 3 in a row
ask.ifNot: A Roman letter may be repeated at most 3 times in a row. Four Xs break the rule, so this is not a proper numeral.

beats.say: So X X X X I X is out. The proper way to write 49 is X L I X.
X X L I V puts two Xs in front of the L. Only one smaller letter may stand in front of a bigger one. So it is out too.
Now the two proper ones. X X X I X is three tens and a nine. That is 39.
X X V I I I is two tens, a five and three ones. That is 28.
39 is more than 28. So the largest is X X X I X.
The trap is to pick the longest numeral, or the one that looks biggest. Check the rules first, then compare the values.
We use 7, 4, 3 and 0, once each, to make 4-digit even numbers. How many can we make?

board.text: Digits 7, 4, 3, 0 once each: how many 4-digit even numbers?

beats.say: An even number ends in an even digit. Which of our digits can go in the last seat?

ask.ifNot: Even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8. From our four digits, 0 and 4 are even. So the last digit is 0 or 4.

beats.say: Group one: the number ends in 0. Then 7, 4 and 3 fill the first three seats in any order. That gives 6 numbers.
Group two: the number ends in 4. The digits left are 7, 3 and 0.
Careful, here is the trap. The first seat cannot be 0, or it is not a 4-digit number. So the first digit is 7 or 3.
That gives 7034, 7304, 3074 and 3704. Just 4 numbers.
Add the two groups: 6 plus 4 is 10.
So: split into cases by the last digit, and leave out anything that starts with 0.
We need to write 1789 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 1000, 700, 80 and 9.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.
1000 is simply M.
Now the 700. How do the Romans write 700?

ask.ifNot: 700 is 500 and 2 more hundreds. The big letter D comes first, and then the two Cs.

beats.say: 700 is 500 and 2 more hundreds, so we write D C C.
80 is 50 and 3 more tens, so we write L X X X. 9 is 1 less than 10, so the smaller letter goes in front: I X.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: M, D C C, L X X X, I X.
The trap here is to write each digit on its own: 1, 7, 8, 9. Roman numerals show the full value of each part, like 1000 and 700.
So the plan for any number: split it by place, write each part in Roman letters, then join them from left to right.
Four Roman numerals, and we want the largest. But be careful: not all of them are proper numerals.

board.text: Which Roman numeral has the largest value?

beats.say: C C D has big letters in it. But two Cs stand in front of the D. Is that allowed?

choices: No, only one letter may go in front
ask.ifNot: Only one smaller letter may stand in front of a bigger one. So C C D is not a proper numeral. 300 is written C C C.

beats.say: So C C D is out. And X X X X I X has X four times in a row, which is not allowed either. Out as well.
Now the proper ones. In X L V I, X L is 10 less than 50, so it is 40. Then V I is 6. That makes 46.
X X V I I I is two tens, a five and three ones. That is 28.
46 is more than 28. So the largest is X L V I.
Notice that X L V I is the shortest proper numeral here, and still the largest. Length tells you nothing.
So: rules first, values second.
Two numbers are given in words. We write them in figures, subtract, and then find the digit in the ten thousands place.

board.text: Difference of the two numbers: ten thousands digit = ?

beats.say: Ninety seven lakh, forty three thousand, seven hundred fifty three. In figures that is 97,43,753.
Forty nine thousand, six hundred eighty two is 49,682.
Now subtract. Line the numbers up by place, ones under ones, and take care with the borrowing.
The difference is 96,94,071. Counting from the right, which seat is the ten thousands place?

ask.ifNot: Count them: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands. That is the 5th seat from the right.

beats.say: Count the seats of 96,94,071 from the right: 1, 7, 0, 4, and then 9.
So the digit in the ten thousands place is 9.
Careful: there are two 9s in the answer, and a 0 too. Always count the seats from the right, one at a time.
We use 3, 4, 5 and 7, once each. We count the numbers that are odd and also greater than 5000.

board.text: Digits 3, 4, 5, 7 once each: odd numbers above 5000?

beats.say: Two rules. To be greater than 5000, the first digit must be 5 or 7. To be odd, the last digit must be 3, 5 or 7.
Suppose the first digit is 5. Which digits can go last?

ask.ifNot: The 5 is already used in the first seat, and each digit is used only once. So the last digit can be 3 or 7.

beats.say: This is the key idea. A digit used in front cannot be used again at the end.
Start with 5 and end with 3: the middle is 4 and 7, in 2 orders. Start with 5 and end with 7: the middle is 3 and 4, in 2 orders.
That is 4 numbers starting with 5. Starting with 7 works the same way: the last digit is 3 or 5.
4 numbers start with 5 and 4 start with 7. That makes 8.
So: fix the first digit, then the last, then count the middle. And never use a digit twice.
We need to write 1997 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 1000, 900, 90 and 7.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.
1000 is simply M. 900 is 100 less than 1000, so the smaller letter goes in front: C M.
Now the 90. How do the Romans write 90?

ask.ifNot: A letter can repeat only 3 times, so L X X X X is not allowed. 90 is 10 less than 100: X before C.

beats.say: 90 is 10 less than 100, so the smaller letter goes in front: X C.
7 is 5 and 2 more, so we write V I I.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: M, C M, X C, V I I.
The same rule made our 900. Not D C C C C, but C before M. Short and neat.
So the plan for any number: split it by place, write each part in Roman letters, then join them from left to right.
Here is 3,62,489. We want to know how much its 6 is really worth.
Count the seats from the right: 9 is in the ones, 8 in the tens, 4 in the hundreds and 2 in the thousands.
The 6 comes next. Which seat is it in?

ask.ifNot: After the thousands seat comes the ten-thousands seat. The 2 is in the thousands, so the 6 is in the ten-thousands.

beats.say: The ten-thousands seat is worth 10,000. So we multiply 6 by 10,000.
6 times 10,000 is 60,000. That is the place value of the 6.
Careful: 6 on its own is just the face value. The place value counts the seat as well.
A quick check: 4 digits come after the 6, so its value is a 6 followed by 4 zeros.
The successor of a number is the very next number. So we add 1 to 99,999.
What happens to a 9 when we add 1 to it?

choices: it becomes 10 in the same seat
ask.ifNot: 9 plus 1 is 10. A seat can hold only one digit, so we write 0 and carry the 1 to the next seat.

beats.say: The 9 in the ones becomes 0 and carries 1. That carry turns the next 9 into 0 as well, and so on, like falling dominoes.
All five 9s become 0, and the last carry makes a brand new 1 in front.
So the successor is 1,00,000. That is one lakh.
Notice that it has 6 digits now. The largest 5-digit number, plus 1, is the smallest 6-digit number.
Careful: 99,998 is the number before. Successor means after, so we add.
4 numbers that look very alike. To find the largest, we compare them seat by seat, starting from the left.
All four start with 4 and then 5. So the first two seats are a tie, and we move on to the hundreds.
The hundreds digits are 0, 3, 3 and 2. Which numbers are still in the race?

ask.ifNot: The biggest hundreds digit is 3. Two numbers have it: 45,302 and 45,320.

beats.say: 3 is the biggest hundreds digit, so 45,032 and 45,203 drop out.
Now compare the tens of the two that are left. 45,302 has 0 tens. 45,320 has 2 tens.
So the largest is 45,320.
So the plan: start at the left, and move one seat to the right only when there is a tie.
Here is a Roman numeral: C D X L I V. We need to turn it into our own numbers.
Here is what each Roman letter is worth.
The secret: when a smaller letter stands before a bigger one, we take it away. This numeral is made of 3 pairs like that.
Take the first pair. C is 100 and D is 500, and the C comes first. So what is C D worth?

ask.ifNot: The smaller letter is in front, so we take it away: 500 minus 100 is 400.

beats.say: 500 minus 100 is 400. So C D is 400.
The next pairs work the same way. X L is 50 minus 10, which is 40. I V is 5 minus 1, which is 4.
Now add the three parts: 400 and 40 and 4.
So C D X L I V is 444.
Careful: if you add every pair instead of taking away, each part comes out too big. Smaller letter in front means take away.
We need to write 789 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 700, 80 and 9.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.
700 is 500 and 2 more hundreds, so we write D C C.
Now the 80. How do the Romans write 80?

ask.ifNot: 80 is 50 and 3 more tens. So we write L, and then three Xs.

beats.say: 80 is 50 and 3 more tens, so we write L X X X.
9 is 1 less than 10, so the smaller letter goes in front: I X.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: D C C, L X X X, I X.
Count the Xs carefully. L X X is only 70, and X C is 90.
So the plan for any number: split it by place, write each part in Roman letters, then join them from left to right.
We round 4,567 to the nearest hundred. First: which two hundreds does it sit between?
It is between 4,500 and 4,600.
To choose between them, which digit of 4,567 do we look at?

ask.ifNot: To round to the hundreds, look at the digit just to the right of the hundreds. That is the tens digit, 6.

beats.say: The tens digit is 6. The rule: 5 or more, round up. Less than 5, round down.
6 is more than 5, so we round up to 4,600.
It makes sense: 4,567 is past the halfway mark, 4,550, so it is nearer to 4,600.
Careful: 4,570 is rounding to the nearest ten. For the nearest hundred, the last two digits both become 0.
How many digits does 5,43,21,678 have? The commas make it easy to count in groups.
The commas split the number into 4 groups: 5, then 43, then 21, then 678.
How many digits are in the last group, 678?

ask.ifNot: 6, 7 and 8. That is 3 digits. In the Indian system the last group always has 3 digits.

beats.say: So the groups have 1, 2, 2 and 3 digits. Add them up.
The number has 8 digits.
Careful: commas are not digits. Count only the digits between them.
Check: write it without commas, 54321678, and count. 8 digits.
Expanded form means we break 30,507 into the value of each digit, and write the values as a sum.
The 3 is in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 30,000.
Next is a 0 in the thousands place. What does it add to the number?

ask.ifNot: 0 thousands is nothing at all. The zero only holds the seat, so that the 3 stays in the ten-thousands place.

beats.say: A zero adds nothing, so we skip it. The 5 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 500.
Another 0 in the tens, so we skip again. The 7 is in the ones, so it is worth 7.
Put the three values together as a sum.
Careful: 30,000 plus 507 also makes 30,507, but 507 is not fully broken up. Expanded form splits every digit.
Ascending means going up, smallest first. All 4 numbers use the same digits, so we compare them seat by seat.
All four have 5 thousands, so that is a tie. Look at the hundreds digits: 4, 3, 4 and 2.
Which number has the smallest hundreds digit?

ask.ifNot: The hundreds digits are 4, 3, 4 and 2. The smallest is 2, and that belongs to 5,234.

beats.say: 5,234 is the smallest, with 2 hundreds. Next is 5,342, with 3 hundreds.
Two numbers have 4 hundreds: 5,432 and 5,423. Break the tie with the tens. 2 tens is less than 3 tens, so 5,423 comes first.
So from smallest to largest, here is the order.
Careful: descending is the other way round, largest first. Always check which order is asked for.
We have the digits 7, 0, 3 and 5, and we use each one once. We want the largest number we can build.
Which seat matters most for making a number large?

ask.ifNot: The seat on the far left is worth the most. One thousand beats all the hundreds, tens and ones we could put here.

beats.say: So the biggest digit, 7, goes in the thousands seat.
Then the next biggest, 5, in the hundreds. Then 3 in the tens. And 0 is left for the ones.
The largest number is 7,530.
Careful: 7,503 looks close. But 3 tens and 0 ones is more than 0 tens and 3 ones.
So for the largest number, write the digits from biggest to smallest.
The predecessor is the number just before. So we take 1 away from 10,000.
Will the answer have 5 digits, like 10,000?

ask.ifNot: 10,000 is the smallest 5-digit number. Anything before it must have fewer digits, so the answer has 4 digits.

beats.say: 10,000 is the smallest number with 5 digits. One step back, and we land on the largest number with 4 digits.
The largest 4-digit number has a 9 in every seat.
So the predecessor is 9,999.
Check by adding back: 9,999 plus 1 is 10,000.
Careful: 10,001 is the successor, the number after. Predecessor means before.
In 4,562, the digit 5 has two values: a place value and a face value. We want the difference between them.

board.text: 4,562: place value of 5 − face value of 5 = ?

beats.say: Which of these is the face value of the 5?

ask.ifNot: Face value is the easy one. It is just the digit itself, wherever it sits. So the face value is 5.

beats.say: The face value is simply 5.
For the place value, find the seat. From the right: 2 ones, 6 tens, 5 hundreds. So it is 5 times 100, which is 500.
Now the difference: 500 minus 5 is 495.
Careful: 500 and 5 are both among the choices. But the question wants the difference between them.
So remember: place value uses the seat, and face value ignores it.
One of these four is not a proper Roman numeral. Each one puts a smaller letter in front of a bigger one, so let us check that rule.

board.text: Which is NOT a valid Roman numeral?

beats.say: A smaller letter in front means take away. But only I, X and C are allowed to do that.

board.text: May go in front to take away: I, X, C

beats.say: Which letters are never used to take away?

ask.ifNot: The letters V for 5, L for 50 and D for 500 are never put in front to take away.

beats.say: X L has X in front of L, and X is allowed. That is 50 minus 10, which is 40. Fine.
X I V has I in front of V. Allowed, and it is 14. I X is 9. Both are fine.
In V X, the V stands in front of X. But V is never used to take away. So V X is not valid.
And there is no need for it. 10 minus 5 is 5, and 5 already has its own letter, V.
To estimate this sum, we round each number to the nearest thousand first, and then add the round numbers.
To round 4,891 to the nearest thousand, which digit do we check?

ask.ifNot: Look one seat to the right of the thousands. That is the hundreds digit, which is 8.

beats.say: The hundreds digit is 8. That is 5 or more, so 4,891 rounds up to 5,000.
For 3,207 the hundreds digit is 2. That is less than 5, so it rounds down to 3,000.
Now add the round numbers. 5,000 plus 3,000 is 8,000.
Is that sensible? The exact sum is 8,098, which is close to 8,000. A good estimate.
Careful: one number went up and the other went down. Check each number on its own.
We read 23,45,678 in the Indian system. The commas show us the groups, which are called periods.
From the right, the first comma cuts off 3 digits: 678. Then come groups of 2 digits: 45, and then 23.
678 is the ones period and 45 is the thousands period. What is the period of the 23?

ask.ifNot: In the Indian system the periods go: ones, thousands, lakhs, crores. The third group from the right is lakhs.

beats.say: So 23 is in the lakhs period.
Read each group with its name: twenty-three lakh, forty-five thousand, six hundred seventy-eight.
Careful: million belongs to the international system. And a crore needs 8 digits, but this number has only 7.
So: split at the commas, name each period, and read from the left.
We count the even numbers between 11 and 21. Between means that 11 and 21 themselves are not included.

board.text: Even numbers between 11 and 21: how many?

beats.say: Which is the first even number after 11?

ask.ifNot: 11 is odd. The very next number, 12, ends in 2, so it is even.

beats.say: Start at 12 and jump in twos: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20.
The next jump would land on 22, which is past 21. So we stop at 20.
Count them. There are 5 even numbers.
Careful: do not forget 20. It is less than 21, so it counts.
So: find the first one, jump in twos, and stop before you pass the end.
We use 9, 0, 3, 1 and 7, once each, to build the smallest 5-digit number.
The smallest digit is 0. Can 0 go in the first seat?

choices: No, then it is not a 5-digit number
ask.ifNot: A number that starts with 0 loses a digit, so it would only be a 4-digit number. The first seat needs the next smallest digit.

beats.say: So the first seat takes the next smallest digit, 1.
Now 0 can take the second seat. It is welcome anywhere except the front.
The rest go from smallest to biggest: 3, 7, 9.
The smallest number is 10,379.
Careful: 13,079 puts the 3 before the 0, and that makes it bigger. Get the 0 in as early as you can.
6 empty seats. We want the smallest number that fills all of them.
We want small digits. What is the smallest digit we can put in the first seat?

ask.ifNot: 0 is smaller, but a number cannot begin with 0. So the first seat gets a 1.

beats.say: The first seat takes 1, because a number cannot begin with 0.
Every other seat takes the smallest digit there is, 0.
With Indian commas, that is 1,00,000. One lakh!
A nice check: it is 1 more than 99,999, the largest 5-digit number.
Careful when you count the zeros: a 1, and then exactly 5 zeros.
Here is a long Roman numeral: M C M X C I X. Let us turn it into our own numbers, one part at a time.
Here is what each Roman letter is worth.
First find the pairs where a smaller letter stands before a bigger one. Those are take away pairs: C M, X C and I X.
The M at the front stands alone, so it is 1000. Next comes C M. C is 100 and M is 1000. What is C M worth?

ask.ifNot: The smaller letter C is in front, so we take it away: 1000 minus 100 is 900.

beats.say: 1000 minus 100 is 900. So far we have 1000 and 900.
X C is 100 minus 10, which is 90. I X is 10 minus 1, which is 9.
Now add the four parts.
So M C M X C I X is 1,999.
Careful with X C. It is 90, not 40. 40 would be X L, with an L for 50.
So the plan: find the take away pairs, work out each part, then add the parts.
Two big numbers, and we want a number that lies between them.
Compare them from the left. Both start with the same three digits: 3, 4, 5. Only the endings differ: 678 and 680.
Which whole number comes between 678 and 680?

ask.ifNot: Count up from 678. The next number is 679, and then comes 680. So 679 is in between.

beats.say: 678, then 679, then 680. Only 679 fits in the gap.
Now put the front digits back. The number is 3,45,679.
Check: it is 1 more than 3,45,678 and 1 less than 3,45,680.
Careful: 3,45,677 and 3,45,681 are close neighbours, but they sit outside the gap.
In 4,372 we need two things: the place value of the 4 and the face value of the 7. Then we multiply them.
The 4 is the first digit of 4,372. What is its place value?

ask.ifNot: 4,372 has 4 digits, so the first seat is the thousands. 4 thousands is 4,000.

beats.say: The 4 is in the thousands place, so its place value is 4,000.
Face value is just the digit itself. So the face value of 7 is 7, even though it sits in the tens.
Product means multiply. 4 times 7 is 28, so 4,000 times 7 is 28,000.
Careful: do not use 70 for the 7. The question asks for its face value, not its place value.
So: read which value is asked for each digit, and then do the sum.
How many zeros does 5 crore have? Let us build up to a crore, step by step.

board.text: How many zeros are in 5 crore?

beats.say: One thousand has 3 zeros. One lakh has 5 zeros.
A crore is 100 lakh. Multiplying by 100 adds 2 more zeros. So how many zeros are in 1 crore?

ask.ifNot: A lakh has 5 zeros, and times 100 adds 2 more. 5 plus 2 is 7.

beats.say: 1 crore is a 1 followed by 7 zeros.
For 5 crore, the 1 simply becomes a 5. The zeros stay the same.
So 5 crore has 7 zeros.
Careful: the 5 in front changes nothing about the zeros. 5 crore, 7 crore, 9 crore: they all have 7 zeros.
We are told the digit in each seat. Let us put them into a place value chart, biggest seat first.
4 in the ten-thousands, 0 in the thousands, 3 in the hundreds, 0 in the tens and 8 in the ones.
Two seats hold a 0. Can we leave those zeros out when we write the number?

ask.ifNot: A zero adds nothing, but it keeps every other digit in its proper seat. Leave it out, and the 4 slides down to a smaller seat.

beats.say: Zeros are place holders. Without them the 4 would not stay in the ten-thousands place.
Read the seats from left to right. The number is 40,308.
Check by adding the values: 40,000 plus 300 plus 8.
Careful: 4,308 drops a zero and has only 4 digits. And 40,380 puts the 8 in the tens seat.
Which sign goes in the blank: greater than, less than, or equals? We compare the two numbers seat by seat, from the left.
Both have 5 digits. Both have 6 ten-thousands, and both have 5 thousands. Still a tie.
Now the hundreds. The first number has 4 hundreds and the second has 3. Which number is bigger?

ask.ifNot: 4 hundreds is more than 3 hundreds. Once one seat is bigger, the seats to its right cannot change the result.

beats.say: 4 hundreds beats 3 hundreds. We can stop here: the first number is greater.
The sign for greater than opens towards the bigger number.
Careful: the two numbers use the same digits. But it is the order of the digits that matters, not just which digits they are.
So: go from the left, and the first seat that differs decides.
Just before means 1 less. So we take 1 away from 50,00,000.
50,00,000 ends in 6 zeros. When we take 1 away, what do those zeros become?

ask.ifNot: Think of a smaller sum: 10 minus 1 is 9. The zero has to borrow, and it turns into a 9.

beats.say: It is like 100 minus 1, which is 99. Every zero borrows from its neighbour and turns into a 9.
The 5 in front lends 1 and becomes 4. And all 6 zeros become 9s.
So the number just before is 49,99,999.
Careful: count the 9s. There must be 6 of them, so the answer still has 7 digits.
We use 5, 3, 8 and 1, once each. We want the largest number, but it must be even.
An even number must end in an even digit. Which of our digits are even?

ask.ifNot: 5, 3 and 1 are odd. The only even digit we have is 8.

beats.say: Only 8 is even. So 8 has to go in the ones seat, like it or not.
This is the trap. We would love to put 8 in front, but then the number would end in an odd digit.
The other digits fill the front, biggest first: 5, 3, 1.
The largest even number is 5,318.
Careful: 8,531 is the largest number from these digits, but it ends in 1, so it is odd.
Adding Roman numerals is hard. So we change them into our own numbers, add, and change back.
X I V is a ten and a four. That is 14.
X X V I I I is two tens, a five and three ones. That is 28.
Add them. 14 plus 28 is 42.
42 is 40 and 2. How do the Romans write 40?

ask.ifNot: A letter is never written 4 times in a row. 40 is 10 less than 50, so X goes in front of L.

beats.say: 40 is X L, and 2 is I I. So the total is X L I I.
Careful: X X X X I I adds up to 42 as well, but 4 Xs in a row are not allowed.
So: change to our numbers, add, and change back.
Look at 99307. We want to compare two digits: the 9 in the ten-thousands place and the 9 in the thousands place.

board.text: In 99307: (9 in ten-thousands) is ? times (9 in thousands)

beats.say: Start with the 9 in the ten-thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 9 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 90000.

beats.say: The ten-thousands place is worth 10000, and 9 times 10000 is 90000.
Now the 9 in the thousands place. That seat is worth 1000, so 9 times 1000 is 9000.
How many times means: how many lots of 9000 fit into 90000? Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 9000 fit into 90000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 3 zeros from each, leaving 90 divided by 9.
90 divided by 9 is 10.
So the 9 in the ten-thousands place is worth 10 times the 9 in the thousands place.
Good mathematicians check. 9000 times 10 takes us back to 90000.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second. And notice: each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right.
Here is our number, 12645. We want the place value of the 6 in the hundreds place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 6 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 6 by 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 6 times 100 is 600. So this 6 is worth 600.
Careful: 6 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 600.
A quick check: 600 is 6 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
This is 68457. Let us find out how much the 4 in the hundreds place stands for.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 4 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 4 by 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 4 times 100 is 400. So this 4 is worth 400.
Careful: 4 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 400.
A quick check: 400 is 4 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
We are hunting for the number whose digits add up to 22. Digit sum simply means: add up the digits.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 22?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 54913. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 5 plus 4 plus 9 plus 1 plus 3. That makes 22.

beats.say: 5 plus 4 plus 9 plus 1 plus 3 makes 22. That is the 22 we are looking for!
Now 43148. 4 plus 3 plus 1 plus 4 plus 8 makes 20. That is less than 22, so not this one.
Now 41608. 4 plus 1 plus 6 plus 0 plus 8 makes 19. That is less than 22, so not this one.
Next, 19149. 1 plus 9 plus 1 plus 4 plus 9 makes 24. That is more than 22, so not this one.
So the number with a digit sum of 22 is 54913.
A tip for next time: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip over it. And check every choice, so nothing surprises you.
Here is 42338. Two digits are marked: the 2 in the thousands place and the 8 in the units place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 42338: (2 in thousands) is ? times (8 in units)

beats.say: Start with the 2 in the thousands place. What is it worth?
